notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **Job 22** — Eliphaz’s third and final speech, his most direct and harsh attack on Job.

---

## Overview of the Chapter

Eliphaz’s third speech is his sharpest. He moves from general theological hints to explicit, invented accusations. The chapter falls into three sections: (1) vv. 1–11 — Eliphaz argues God gains nothing from human righteousness, then lists fabricated sins; (2) vv. 12–20 — he accuses Job of practical atheism, likening him to the wicked of Noah’s day; (3) vv. 21–30 — a call to repentance couched in beautiful promises, true in themselves but wrongly applied since Job had not abandoned God. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/ ; Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-22.html)

---

## Verse-by-Verse Notes

**v. 1: “Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied…”**
Eliphaz leads the third cycle of speeches. He is likely the eldest and regarded as the wisest of the three friends, so he speaks first each round. Gill notes that in this third speech he abandons reasoned argument, turning instead to calumny and reproach. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm)

**v. 2: “Can a man be of use to God? Can even a wise man benefit Him?”**
Eliphaz asserts God’s self-sufficiency: man cannot profit God. Gill says this is a “very great truth, though misapplied to Job.” Matthew Henry concurs: “Man’s piety is no profit to God, no gain… Our wisdom and piety are that by which we ourselves are great gainers.” Eliphaz imagines Job thought God owed him something for his righteousness. The theology — God needs nothing — is orthodox, but Eliphaz misapplies it, ignoring that God Himself took pleasure in Job’s righteousness (Job 1–2). (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**v. 3: “Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous? Does He profit if your ways are blameless?”**
Eliphaz presses further: God takes no pleasure in human righteousness and gains nothing from it. Gill explains that while God does take pleasure in His people’s righteousness, it adds no new happiness to Him — He would have been equally blessed without any righteous man on earth. Enduring Word notes that Eliphaz’s theology here echoes Zophar’s earlier argument (Job 11) on grounds akin to what would later be called Reformed or Calvinistic theology — God’s sovereignty and self-existence — but wrongly applied to Job’s situation, since God *did* delight in Job’s blamelessness. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**v. 4: “Is it for your reverence that He rebukes you and enters into judgment against you?”**
Eliphaz’s point is sarcastic: “Does God afflict you *because* you fear Him?” The obvious answer is no — therefore Job must be afflicted for his sins. Gill paraphrases: God does not chastise out of fear that Job might harm Him, nor out of respect for Job’s piety. Matthew Henry adds: “God rebukes the good because he loves them, but he never rebukes the great because he fears them.” Ellicott renders it: “Because He standeth in awe of thee.” (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm)

**v. 5: “Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?”**
Here Eliphaz shifts from theology to direct accusation. He cannot conceive that suffering so severe could befall an innocent man, so Job’s wickedness must be enormous. Ellicott calls this “mere conjecture and surmise, arising simply from a false assumption: namely, that a just God can only punish the wicked.” Enduring Word notes that Eliphaz’s only evidence was Job’s catastrophic condition — he had no actual proof. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**v. 6: “For you needlessly demanded security from your brothers and deprived the naked of their clothing.”**
The first specific (and false) charge: taking pledges (security) from a brother for a trivial debt, even stripping the poor of their garments. Gill notes that the Law of Moses later forbade keeping a poor man’s cloak overnight (Ex. 22:26). Matthew Henry calls this utterly false, pointing to Job’s own self-defence in ch. 29 and God’s commendation in ch. 1. The Monergism article says these were “fabrications, born out of the false assumption that suffering is always the direct result of personal wrongdoing.” (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm ; Monergism: https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/failure-job%E2%80%99s-friends-warning-against-misrepresenting-god)

**v. 7: “You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished.”**
Eliphaz accuses Job of hard-heartedness toward the needy. Matthew Henry observes this is contrary to Job’s later testimony: “I have not withheld the poor from their desire” (Job 31:16–17). Enduring Word calls this “a remarkable list of groundless accusations… mainly of greed and cruelty.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/ ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm)

**v. 8: “while the land belonged to a mighty man, and a man of honor lived on it.”**
Interpretations differ. Gill suggests Eliphaz means that Job, as “the mighty man” (literally “man of arm”), used his power to seize land and property by force. Ellicott likewise takes “the mighty and the honourable man” as referring to Job himself. This intensifies the charge: Job abused his position of power. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm)

**v. 9: “You sent widows away empty-handed, and the strength of the fatherless was crushed.”**
Eliphaz charges Job with cruelty to widows and orphans — the most vulnerable. Gill explains “the arms of the fatherless have been broken” is metaphorical: their substance was taken, leaving them helpless. Matthew Henry notes that Eliphaz does not outright say “thou hast broken them” but insinuates it, as though Job connived at it. (Gill: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/job-22.html ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm)

**vv. 10–11: “Therefore snares surround you… it is so dark you cannot see, and a flood of water covers you.”**
Eliphaz presents Job’s calamities as the direct consequence of these supposed sins. Snares, sudden fear, darkness, and overwhelming flood waters — these are the just deserts of the oppressor. Enduring Word notes that the images of darkness and flood are “the best examples of God’s judgment,” though they don’t match the events of chapters 1–2. Matthew Henry adds a pastoral insight: “Those that have not shown mercy may justly be denied the comfortable hope that they shall find mercy.” (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/ ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm)

**vv. 12–14: “Is not God as high as the heavens? … Yet you say: ‘What does God know? Does He judge through thick darkness?’”**
Eliphaz now accuses Job of practical atheism — denying God’s knowledge of earthly affairs because He dwells in the high heavens behind thick clouds. Matthew Henry explains: Eliphaz thinks Job reasons, “God is too high and too busy enjoying heaven to trouble Himself with us.” This is a grave misrepresentation; Job never said this. Ellicott notes that Eliphaz attributes to Job the very sentiments he earlier ascribed to the wicked man (Job 21:14–15). The Pulpit Commentary says Eliphaz “proceeds to accuse him of denying God’s omniscience.” (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm ; Pulpit Commentary excerpt: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/job-22.html)

**vv. 15–16: “Will you stay on the ancient path that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time, and their foundations were swept away by a flood.”**
Eliphaz asks whether Job intends to persist in the “old way” of the wicked. Most older commentators see here an allusion to Noah’s flood. Ellicott says the reference to being “cut down out of time” and “whose foundation was overflown with a flood” is “generally supposed to be an allusion to the history of the Flood,” which he notes is “very important in its bearing on the age of that record, since the Book of Job can hardly fail to be very old itself.” John Trapp also suggested a reference to Sodom’s destruction by fire and brimstone. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**vv. 17–18: “They said to God, ‘Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?’ But it was He who filled their houses with good things…”**
These are the words of the wicked before the flood: they told God to leave them alone, questioning what the Almighty could do. Yet God had filled their houses with good things — making their defiance all the more ungrateful. Matthew Henry notes the irony: they lived on God’s bounty while banishing Him from their thoughts. Ellicott detects bitter irony in Eliphaz adopting the very formula of repudiation that Job himself had used (Job 21:16). When Eliphaz says “the counsel of the wicked is far from me,” he implies Job’s counsel is that of the wicked. (Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm)

**vv. 19–20: “The righteous see it and are glad; the innocent mock them: ‘Surely our foes are destroyed, and fire has consumed their excess.’”**
Eliphaz contrasts the righteous who rejoice in God’s judgment on the wicked with Job, who does not. This implies Job is among the wicked. Matthew Henry clarifies that the righteous rejoice not in human misery but in seeing God glorified, His word fulfilled, and oppression broken. The “fire” probably alludes to Sodom’s destruction — a second great judgment alongside the flood. (Matthew Henry: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/job/22.htm ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm)

**v. 21: “Reconcile now and be at peace with Him; thereby good will come to you.”**
A dramatic transition: Eliphaz turns from accusation to tender exhortation. The advice is “exquisite” (Meyer, cited by Enduring Word) — but it assumes Job has left God, which he has not. The Pulpit Commentary notes that Eliphaz falls back on the themes of his first speech (Job 5:8–27), calling Job to return to God. The Hebrew implies a thorough, effectual turning. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/ ; Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm)

**v. 22: “Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart.”**
Eliphaz urges Job to receive God’s *torah* (instruction/law) and treasure it internally. Ellicott raises the intriguing question of whether the word *torah* here alludes to the Mosaic Law. He concludes that Job probably predates the giving of the Law and that “His words” likely refer to the inner revelation of God’s voice in conscience. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm)

**v. 23: “If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored. If you remove injustice from your tents…”**
Eliphaz promises restoration upon repentance. The Hebrew for “you will be built up” suggests reconstruction of a ruin. Constable notes: “Job did not need to repent, as Eliphaz suggested. He was not suffering because he had sinned greatly.” The James Smith devotional (Precept Austin) reads into this a “renewal of the nature” — the spiritual nature broken by sin being rebuilt by God. (Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-22.html ; James Smith via Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/job-commentary-james-smith)

**v. 24: “and consign your gold to the dust and the gold of Ophir to the stones of the ravines…”**
Ellicott explains: Eliphaz tells Job to treat his treasure as worthless as dust and stream-bed stones — i.e., stop setting his heart on wealth. Ophir’s location is disputed (Josephus placed it in India; others suggest southern Arabia or East Africa). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Eliphaz seems to imply Job’s wealth was ill-gotten gain. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm)

**v. 25: “then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you.”**
This is among the most sublime statements in the book. The Almighty Himself becomes the believer’s true treasure. Ellicott renders the Hebrew: “And the Almighty shall be thy treasure, and precious silver unto thee.” Enduring Word notes that the promise is true in itself — God is indeed better than gold. (Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**v. 26: “Surely then you will delight in the Almighty and lift up your face to God.”**
Eliphaz describes the joy of restored fellowship: the downcast face of guilt is lifted toward God. The Pulpit Commentary elaborates: “God shall no longer be a terror and alarm to thee… but a source of rejoicing.” John Piper (Desiring God) focused his sermon *“What Is It Like to Enjoy God?”* on these verses, calling the statement true and beautiful: “If God is your gold, he will be your gladness.” Yet Piper also notes that God was angry with Eliphaz (Job 42:7) because he used truth as a cruel indictment against a good man. (Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm ; Piper via Desiring God search result: https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/job/22/messages)

**v. 27: “You will pray to Him, and He will hear you, and you will fulfill your vows.”**
Eliphaz promises answered prayer. Job currently prays but feels unheard; Eliphaz says repentance will open God’s ear. The Pulpit Commentary adds: “Thou shalt have wealth enough, and strength enough, to pay any vows that thou hast made, which now in thy afflicted state thou canst not do.” (Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm)

**v. 28: “Your decisions will be carried out, and light will shine on your ways.”**
Whatever Job decrees, God will establish. Job had complained of darkness on his path (Job 19:8); Eliphaz promises the light will return. The Pulpit Commentary notes “a touch of audacity” in this sweeping promise, comparing it to Psalm 37:4–5. (Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm)

**v. 29: “When men are brought low and you say, ‘Lift them up!’ then He will save the lowly.”**
Job will become an intercessor for the humble. The Pulpit Commentary’s alternative reading: “When men are cast down, then thou shalt say, Let there be lifting up.” (Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm)

**v. 30: “He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands.”**
Eliphaz’s final words are prophetic in a way he could not have foreseen. The Hebrew (אִי for אֵין) means “him that is not innocent.” The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both note the remarkable irony: Eliphaz himself would later need Job’s intercession to be delivered from God’s wrath (Job 42:7–9). Eliphaz prophesied his own deliverance through “the pureness of Job’s hands.” Enduring Word calls this “a stunning reversal of roles.” (Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/job/22.htm ; Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/22.htm ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

---

## Points of Protestant Debate and Distinctive Readings

**Reformed / Calvinistic:** The Monergism article highlights that Eliphaz and his friends held a “rigid and simplistic understanding of God’s justice” — a strict retribution theology: the righteous prosper, the wicked suffer. This error “led them into another grave mistake: not only did they misrepresent the ways of God, but they also slandered Job.” The Reformed emphasis is on God’s sovereignty and mystery in suffering, which the friends failed to grasp. Enduring Word (David Guzik, broadly Reformed-leaning charismatic) notes that in vv. 2–3 Eliphaz takes up arguments “upon similar lines” to what would become Calvinistic theology — stressing divine transcendence and self-sufficiency — but misapplies them. (Monergism: https://www.monergism.com/reformation-theology/blog/failure-job%E2%80%99s-friends-warning-against-misrepresenting-god ; Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-22/)

**Baptist / John Piper (Desiring God):** Piper focuses on vv. 24–26 as containing profound truth about delighting in God above all earthly treasure (Christian Hedonism). He stresses that the *content* of Eliphaz’s counsel — “the Almighty will be your gold” — is biblically true, but it was spoken as an indictment, making God angry (Job 42:7). This serves as a warning that true theology can be weaponised. Piper also notes in another message that Eliphaz’s accusations in vv. 5–9 are flat lies, exposing how bad theology distorts reality and hurts people. (Piper messages on Job 22 via Desiring God search results: https://www.desiringgod.org/scripture/job/22/messages ; sermon excerpt: https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/holding-on-to-your-faith-in-the-midst-of-suffering-job-part-2)

**Evangelical / Dispensational (Constable):** Constable warns that Eliphaz’s appeal in vv. 21–30 should not be used as a model for evangelism: “God does not require reformation before He will accept a sinner. Furthermore, He does not promise physical prosperity to those who repent.” This counters any prosperity-gospel reading of the chapter. (Constable via StudyLight: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-22.html)

**Methodist / Wesleyan, Pentecostal, Lutheran, Anglican:** No tradition-specific commentary on Job 22 was found from the designated sites (seedbed.com, ag.org, lcms.org, 1517.org, spurgeon.org, gty.org) in the available searches. The traditional readings given above (Matthew Henry, Ellicott, Pulpit, Gill) represent a broadly shared Protestant consensus.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on Job 22 was found on newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search constraints. The traditional Christian reading of this chapter is largely shared across traditions: Eliphaz speaks partial truth but fundamentally misrepresents both God and Job.

**Modern Scholarship:** No results were retrieved from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the search constraints. 

**On Prosperity Teaching:** Though no prosperity-gospel site was searched, Constable’s note is relevant: Eliphaz’s promise of material restoration upon repentance (vv. 23–25) is *not* a universal biblical promise. “He does not promise physical prosperity to those who repent. Again, Eliphaz’s basic retribution theology led him to misrepresent God and misunderstand life” (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-22.html). Eliphaz’s error — that righteousness always yields wealth and sin always yields poverty — is the very premise prosperity teachers adopt, and the book of Job as a whole dismantles it.
